name: Cave painting
desc: Images painted on cave walls with ochre and charcoal, among the oldest surviving forms of symbolic visual communication.

name: Petroglyph
desc: Images pecked or carved into rock surfaces, used across the world to record and convey meaning.

name: Proto-writing
desc: Systems of conventional symbols, such as marks on tokens and pottery, that carried information before full writing.

name: Cylinder seal
desc: Carved stone cylinders rolled onto clay to impress images, an early form of repeatable printing and authentication.

name: Clay tablet
desc: Tablets of wet clay inscribed and then dried or fired, the main writing medium of Mesopotamia.

name: Stylus
desc: A pointed or wedge-tipped tool for marking clay or wax, the first dedicated writing instrument.

name: Cuneiform
desc: Wedge-shaped Mesopotamian script pressed into clay, used for three millennia across many languages.

name: Egyptian hieroglyphs
desc: Formal Egyptian writing system combining logographic and phonetic signs, carved on monuments and written on papyrus.

name: Ink
desc: Pigment or dye suspended in liquid, first made from soot and gum, that let writing be done quickly on soft surfaces.

name: Reed pen
desc: A cut reed used to write ink on papyrus, the standard pen of the ancient Mediterranean world.

name: Scroll
desc: Long rolls of papyrus or leather that served as the main book format in antiquity.

name: Mail
desc: Organized delivery of written messages by courier, later developed into state relay and public postal systems.

name: Bamboo and wooden slips
desc: Strips of bamboo or wood bound with cord, the main writing medium in China before paper.

name: Wax tablet
desc: A wooden board coated in wax for reusable notes, widely used in Greece and Rome.

name: Smoke signal
desc: Visual signals made with smoke or beacon fires to pass warnings over long distances.

name: Parchment
desc: Prepared animal skin used as a durable writing surface, popularized at Pergamon.

name: Codex
desc: Book made of stacked sheets bound along one edge, which replaced the scroll and allowed random access to text.

name: Iron gall ink
desc: Permanent ink made from iron salts and tannins, the standard European writing ink for over a thousand years.

name: Quill
desc: A pen cut from a bird feather, the main Western writing tool from late antiquity to the 19th century.

name: Woodblock printing
desc: Printing from carved wooden blocks, developed in China and used for the first printed books.

name: Intaglio printmaking
desc: Printing from images incised into a metal plate, used for engravings, maps and banknotes.

name: Pencil
desc: Writing tool with a graphite core, later encased in wood, that made erasable marks.

name: Newspaper
desc: Regularly printed publication of news, first issued in Strasbourg, that created a mass reading public.

name: Magic lantern
desc: An early image projector that threw painted glass slides onto a screen, ancestor of the film projector.

name: Optical telegraph
desc: Chappe's network of semaphore towers that relayed coded messages across France in minutes.

name: Lithography
desc: Printing from a flat stone or plate using the repulsion of oil and water, invented by Alois Senefelder.

name: Paper machine
desc: Machine that forms paper as a continuous web, the Fourdrinier type made paper cheap and plentiful.

name: Dip pen
desc: Pen with a mass-produced steel nib dipped in ink, which replaced the quill in the 19th century.

name: Braille
desc: Tactile writing system of raised dots devised by Louis Braille for blind readers.

name: Fountain pen
desc: Pen with an internal ink reservoir fed to the nib by capillary action.

name: Phenakistiscope
desc: Spinning disc of sequential drawings that produced the illusion of motion, the first widespread animation device.

name: Morse code
desc: Code of dots and dashes for letters and numbers that became the global standard for telegraphy.

name: Daguerreotype
desc: First commercially practical photographic process, producing detailed unique images on silvered copper.

name: Postage stamp
desc: Prepaid adhesive stamp, introduced with Britain's Penny Black, that enabled cheap uniform postal rates.

name: Calotype
desc: Talbot's paper negative process, the first to allow multiple prints from one exposure.

name: Fax
desc: Transmission of scanned images over wires, first patented by Alexander Bain.

name: Rotary printing press
desc: Press with type or plates on a rotating cylinder, enabling very fast newspaper printing.

name: Printing telegraph
desc: Telegraph that printed received messages as text, removing the need for trained operators to read code.

name: Submarine communications cable
desc: Insulated cable laid on the seabed to carry telegraph signals between landmasses.

name: Collodion process
desc: Wet-plate glass negative process that cut exposure times and dominated photography for 30 years.

name: Phonautograph
desc: Scott's device that traced sound waves onto paper, the first recording of sound, though it could not play back.

name: Transatlantic telegraph cable
desc: Undersea cable linking Europe and North America, reliably operating from 1866.

name: Color photography
desc: Reproduction of colors in photographs, first demonstrated by Maxwell's three-color projection.

name: Pantelegraph
desc: Caselli's image telegraph, the first commercial fax service, operating between Paris and Lyon.

name: Ticker tape
desc: Telegraph printer that output stock prices on paper strip, giving markets near-real-time quotes.

name: Typewriter
desc: Machine that printed characters by striking inked ribbon, transforming office work and writing.

name: Dry plate
desc: Gelatin silver halide plate that could be stored before use, enabling factory-made photographic materials.

name: QWERTY
desc: Keyboard layout devised for the Sholes and Glidden typewriter that remains the standard today.

name: Baudot code
desc: Five-bit character code for telegraphy, a forerunner of digital character encoding.

name: Offset printing
desc: Lithographic printing via a rubber blanket cylinder, which became the dominant commercial printing method.

name: Microphone
desc: Transducer converting sound into an electrical signal, first developed for telephony.

name: Phonograph
desc: Edison's machine that recorded and replayed sound from grooves on a cylinder.

name: Carbon microphone
desc: Microphone using carbon granules whose resistance varies with pressure, standard in telephones for a century.

name: Telephone exchange
desc: Central switchboard where operators connected calls between subscribers.

name: Chronophotography
desc: Sequential photographs capturing phases of motion, pioneered by Muybridge and Marey.

name: Halftone
desc: Process rendering photographs as dots of varying size so they could be printed alongside text.

name: Nipkow disk
desc: Spinning disc with spiral holes that scanned images line by line, the basis of mechanical television.

name: Linotype machine
desc: Keyboard machine that cast whole lines of type in hot metal, speeding newspaper composition.

name: Roll film
desc: Flexible film wound on a spool, allowing many exposures without changing plates.

name: Antenna
desc: Conductor that radiates or captures radio waves, first used by Hertz to demonstrate electromagnetic waves.

name: Gramophone record
desc: Berliner's flat disc record, which could be mass-pressed and became the dominant recording medium.

name: Kodak camera
desc: Eastman's 1888 Kodak, a simple box camera sold loaded with roll film, which brought photography to amateurs.

name: Celluloid film
desc: Transparent flexible celluloid base coated with emulsion, which made motion pictures possible.

name: Strowger switch
desc: First automatic telephone exchange switch, letting callers connect without an operator.

name: Kinetoscope
desc: Edison and Dickson's peephole viewer for moving pictures on film.

name: 35 mm movie film
desc: Perforated 35 mm film gauge introduced by Dickson that became the worldwide cinema standard.

name: Cinématographe
desc: Lumière brothers' camera and projector, used for the first public paying film screenings.

name: Wire recording
desc: Poulsen's magnetic recording of sound on steel wire, the first magnetic recording.

name: Loading coil
desc: Inductors placed along telephone lines to reduce distortion, extending long-distance calls.

name: Rotary dial
desc: Finger-wheel dial sending pulses to automatic exchanges, letting subscribers dial their own calls.

name: Crystal detector
desc: Semiconductor crystal contact that rectified radio signals, the first semiconductor device.

name: Amplitude modulation
desc: Varying a carrier wave's strength with a signal, which first allowed voice and music to be sent by radio.

name: Autochrome Lumière
desc: First commercially successful color photography process, using dyed potato starch grains.

name: Color motion picture film
desc: Film recording color moving images, first commercially with Kinemacolor.

name: Teleprinter
desc: Electromechanical typewriter sending and receiving text over wires, used for news wires and business.

name: Headphones
desc: Small loudspeakers worn over the ears, first used by radio and telephone operators.

name: Regenerative circuit
desc: Armstrong's positive-feedback amplifier that made radio receivers far more sensitive.

name: Superheterodyne receiver
desc: Receiver that converts signals to a fixed intermediate frequency, the design used by nearly all radios since.

name: Frequency-division multiplexing
desc: Carrying many calls on one line on separate carrier frequencies, the basis of long-distance carrier systems.

name: Crossbar switch
desc: Matrix switch used in automatic exchanges, faster and more reliable than step-by-step switches.

name: Radio broadcasting
desc: Scheduled transmission of programs to a mass audience, beginning with stations like KDKA.

name: Wirephoto
desc: Transmission of news photographs over telephone lines, letting papers print same-day pictures.

name: Sound-on-film
desc: Recording of a soundtrack as an optical track alongside the film images.

name: Shortwave radio
desc: Radio using high frequencies that reflect off the ionosphere, enabling intercontinental broadcasting.

name: Moving-coil loudspeaker
desc: Rice and Kellogg's moving-coil speaker, the design still used to reproduce sound in most loudspeakers.

name: Mechanical television
desc: Television using spinning discs to scan images, first demonstrated by Baird.

name: Sound film
desc: Motion pictures with synchronized recorded sound, which transformed cinema after The Jazz Singer.

name: Videotelephony
desc: Two-way transmission of video and audio between users, first demonstrated by AT&T in 1927.

name: Magnetic tape
desc: Plastic or paper tape coated with magnetic particles, the basis of audio, video and data recording.

name: Terrestrial television
desc: Over-the-air television broadcasting from ground transmitters to home receivers.

name: Coaxial cable
desc: Shielded cable with a central conductor that carries high-frequency signals with low loss.

name: Microwave relay
desc: Point-to-point radio links at microwave frequencies, later used for nationwide telephone and TV networks.

name: Stereophonic sound
desc: Blumlein's two-channel sound reproduction that creates a spatial impression of sources.

name: Technicolor
desc: Three-strip color film process that defined color cinema from the 1930s to the 1950s.

name: Frequency modulation
desc: Armstrong's method of varying carrier frequency, giving radio far lower static than AM.

name: Iconoscope
desc: Electronic camera tube by Zworykin that made practical television cameras possible.

name: Reel-to-reel tape recording
desc: Open-reel magnetic tape recorders such as the Magnetophon, used for broadcast and studio work.

name: Kodachrome
desc: Subtractive color reversal film that made color photography widely accessible.

name: Pulse-code modulation
desc: Reeves's method of sampling and coding analog signals as numbers, the foundation of digital audio and telephony.

name: FM broadcasting
desc: Radio broadcasting with frequency modulation, offering higher fidelity and less noise.

name: Xerography
desc: Carlson's dry copying process using electrostatic charge on a photoconductor and toner powder.

name: Ballpoint pen
desc: Bíró's pen dispensing quick-drying ink via a rolling ball, now the most common writing tool.

name: Walkie-talkie
desc: Handheld two-way radio transceiver, developed for military field use.

name: Frequency-hopping spread spectrum
desc: Rapidly switching carrier frequency to resist jamming, later used in Bluetooth and cellular systems.

name: Mobile Telephone Service
desc: Early vehicle radiotelephone service connected to the public telephone network.

name: LP record
desc: Long-playing microgroove record at 33 1/3 rpm, holding a whole album per side.

name: Instant camera
desc: Land's Polaroid camera that developed prints inside the camera within minutes.

name: Cable television
desc: Delivery of television over coaxial cable, first to reach areas with poor reception.

name: Answering machine
desc: Device that records callers' messages when a telephone goes unanswered.

name: Pager
desc: Small radio receiver that alerts the user to a message, widely used by doctors and businesses.

name: Phototypesetting
desc: Setting type by projecting characters onto photographic paper, replacing hot metal.

name: Inkjet printing
desc: Printing by propelling tiny ink droplets onto paper, first used in chart recorders.

name: Color television
desc: Broadcast television in color, made practical by the backward-compatible NTSC standard.

name: CinemaScope
desc: Anamorphic widescreen film format that popularized wide aspect ratios in cinema.

name: Transistor radio
desc: Small portable radio receiver using transistors, the first mass-market transistor product.

name: Videotape
desc: Magnetic tape recording of television signals, first with Ampex's Quadruplex recorder.

name: TAT-1
desc: First transatlantic telephone cable, with submerged vacuum tube repeaters.

name: Optical fiber
desc: Thin glass fiber that guides light by total internal reflection, the medium of modern long-haul communication.

name: Modem
desc: Device converting digital data to audio tones for transmission over telephone lines.

name: Communications satellite
desc: Satellite that relays radio signals between distant points on Earth.

name: Photocopier
desc: Automatic office copier, launched as the Xerox 914, that made copying instant and ubiquitous.

name: Telstar
desc: First active satellite to relay live transatlantic television and telephone signals.

name: Satellite television
desc: Television delivered via communications satellites, later direct to home dishes.

name: T-carrier
desc: First digital telephone transmission system, multiplexing 24 PCM voice channels on copper pairs.

name: Syncom
desc: First geosynchronous communications satellites, enabling fixed ground antennas.

name: Compact Cassette
desc: Philips's small tape cassette that made recording and portable music widespread.

name: Touch-tone dialing
desc: Signaling digits with pairs of audio tones, replacing pulse dialing on push-button phones.

name: Electronic switching system
desc: First large stored-program telephone switch, controlled by a computer program.

name: OFDM
desc: Spreading data over many closely spaced orthogonal subcarriers, the basis of Wi-Fi, LTE and digital broadcasting.

name: Digital recording
desc: Storing audio as sampled numeric values, first demonstrated by NHK.

name: Charge-coupled device
desc: Semiconductor image sensor that converts light into electronic charge, enabling digital imaging.

name: Laser printer
desc: Printer using a laser to draw an image on a xerographic drum, developed at Xerox PARC.

name: IMAX
desc: Very large film format and projection system for immersive cinema.

name: Videocassette recorder
desc: Recorder using enclosed tape cassettes, bringing video recording to homes.

name: Email
desc: Electronic messages sent between users on networked computers, first between ARPANET hosts.

name: Voice over IP
desc: Carrying voice calls as digital packets over data networks, first tested on ARPANET.

name: Teletext
desc: Text pages of news and information broadcast in the television signal's blanking interval.

name: Digital camera
desc: Camera that records images as digital data, first built at Kodak in 1975.

name: VHS
desc: JVC's home videocassette format that dominated home video for two decades.

name: Fiber-optic communication
desc: Sending information as pulses of light through optical fiber, first carrying live telephone traffic in 1977.

name: LaserDisc
desc: First commercial optical disc, storing analog video read by a laser.

name: Cellular network
desc: Radio network divided into cells that reuse frequencies, allowing mass mobile telephony.

name: 1G
desc: First-generation analog cellular networks such as NTT's in Tokyo and later AMPS.

name: Walkman
desc: Sony's portable cassette player that made personal mobile listening common.

name: Compact disc
desc: Optical disc storing digital audio, which replaced vinyl and cassette as the main music format.

name: Emoticon
desc: Typographic faces such as :-) used to convey tone in text, proposed by Scott Fahlman.

name: Camcorder
desc: Video camera and recorder combined in one portable unit.

name: Desktop publishing
desc: Page layout on personal computers with laser printing, which democratized publishing.

name: TAT-8
desc: First transatlantic fiber-optic cable, greatly increasing intercontinental capacity.

name: Digital subscriber line
desc: Broadband data transmission over ordinary telephone wires at frequencies above voice.

name: High-definition television
desc: Television with substantially more scan lines than standard definition, first broadcast in Japan.

name: 2G
desc: Digital cellular networks led by GSM, adding encryption and text messaging.

name: Webcam
desc: Video camera feeding images to a computer network, first used at Cambridge to watch a coffee pot.

name: SMS
desc: Short text messages sent between mobile phones, which became a dominant form of communication.

name: JPEG
desc: Lossy image compression standard that made digital photographs practical to store and share.

name: MPEG-1
desc: Standard for compressed digital video and audio, which included the MP3 audio format.

name: MP3
desc: Perceptual audio coding format that shrank music files about tenfold, enabling digital music distribution.

name: Streaming media
desc: Delivery of audio and video over a network for playback as it arrives.

name: CMOS image sensor
desc: Image sensor with amplifiers in each pixel, cheaper and lower power than CCDs, used in phone cameras.

name: IS-95 CDMA
desc: First cellular standard based on code-division multiple access, sharing spectrum via spread spectrum codes.

name: MPEG-2
desc: Video compression standard used for DVD and digital television broadcasting.

name: DVD
desc: High-capacity optical disc for digital video, which replaced VHS for home movies.

name: MIMO
desc: Using multiple antennas to transmit parallel data streams, multiplying wireless capacity.

name: Wi-Fi
desc: Wireless local area networking based on IEEE 802.11, now the main way devices connect to the internet.

name: Digital television
desc: Broadcast of television as compressed digital signals, replacing analog transmission.

name: Portable media player
desc: Pocket device for storing and playing digital music files.

name: Emoji
desc: Pictographs embedded in text, first designed for Japanese mobile phones and later standardized in Unicode.

name: Bluetooth
desc: Short-range wireless standard for linking phones, headsets and peripherals.

name: Digital cinema
desc: Production and projection of films digitally instead of on photographic film.

name: Camera phone
desc: Mobile phone with a built-in camera, which made photography constant and instantly shareable.

name: GPRS
desc: Packet data service on GSM networks that brought always-on internet access to phones.

name: 3G
desc: Third-generation cellular networks providing mobile broadband for web and video.

name: H.264
desc: Efficient video compression standard used for Blu-ray, streaming and video calls.

name: Podcast
desc: Episodic digital audio programs distributed over the internet for download or streaming.

name: Blu-ray
desc: High-density optical disc read by a blue-violet laser, storing high-definition video.

name: 4G
desc: All-IP cellular networks based on LTE, offering broadband speeds for smartphones.

name: 5G
desc: Fifth-generation cellular networks with higher speeds, lower latency and millimetre-wave bands.

name: Starlink
desc: SpaceX's low Earth orbit satellite constellation providing broadband internet worldwide.
